about: What a governor's declaration of a state of emergency moves. The power itself is each state's own (data/research/executive/executive-powers-2026.json, canOrder key emergency-declaration). Read by declareEmergency in src/core2/modules/executive.ts.

budgetLine.source: A state's emergency response is paid from its general program spending, which the Census state finance table groups under all other functions (U.S. Census Bureau, State and Local Government Finances 2022, Table 1, Other expenditure).
budgetLine.spread: Public safety (fire protection) in states that fund emergency management there.

nonFederalShare.source: The federal share of Public Assistance is not less than 75 percent of eligible cost, so the non-federal share is 25 percent (Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act sec. 403(b) and 406(b), 42 U.S.C. 5170b and 5172; 44 CFR 206.203(b)).

stateShareOfNonFederal.source: The part of the non-federal cost the state takes on and the rest left to the county and town. States often cover half or more of the local match for declared disasters (NCSL, State Disaster Assistance 2019; Federal Funds Information for States).

briefing.about: Who is in the governor's room when a disaster record lands and the governor is the player: the state cabinet posts (the keys in data/research/executive/executive-powers-2026.json) whose departments the disaster touches, by the incident type of the FEMA declaration record, lead department first. A state without a post has no one in that seat. Any type not listed uses the default. Read by the emergency-briefing scene (src/director/civic-roles.ts) and by emergencyBriefingPosts in src/core2/modules/executive.ts.
briefing.source: Which department answers each kind of disaster is read from the statutes that give it the work: the governor commands the state's National Guard unless it is called into federal service (U.S. Const. art. I, sec. 8, cl. 16); a state emergency declaration is the step before the governor's request for a federal declaration (Stafford Act sec. 401, 42 U.S.C. 5170; 44 CFR 206.36); a biological incident is a public health emergency (42 U.S.C. 247d); a drought is answered by the agriculture department's disaster designations (7 U.S.C. 1961); a hazardous release falls to the environment agency (CERCLA, 42 U.S.C. 9601 et seq.); wildfire help is a Fire Management Assistance Grant (Stafford Act sec. 420, 42 U.S.C. 5187).
briefing.spread: States organize emergency management differently (some place it under the adjutant general, some under public safety, some under the governor's office), so a state's own plan may seat a department this map leaves out or one of these may sit under another.
